articles.text: A Piedmont resident provides feedback on the Parks Sustainable Management Plan at the Piedmont Park pop-up After months of survey work and park pop-ups, Piedmont’s Park Commission is discussing its Sustainable Park Management plan at its meeting on Wednesday, February 4. Over 580 people have engaged with the Park Commission, providing their values and what they’d like to see in Piedmont’s Parks. At Wednesday’s meeting, the commission will discuss the results of its engagement efforts to create guidelines that provide a framework for future decisions that capture what the community values most about the parks. The project analyzes how the city currently cares for its parks and spaces to identify ways they can better align maintenance with sustainable best practices. The plan will not design or build new parks, make decisions about removing activities/amenities, or replace future planning for facilities. The Park Commission is working in cooperation with WRT Design, an interdisciplinary planning and design practice that works with cities and institutions across the Bay Area to plan and create parks. The group has most recently worked with the cities of Tiburon, San Leandro, Oakland, Moraga, and the East Bay Regional Park District. The Park Commission expects to have a finalized management plan in the Spring of this year. Residents can attend the Park Commission meeting starting at 5:30 p.m. at City Hall or watch on KCOM (Channel 27) and on the City’s website: piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: The Beach community gathered on Sunday, February 1, to celebrate the Year of the Horse. Nearly 200 people attended, making it the best turnout yet for the annual Lunar New Year celebration organized by the Beach Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging Committee. Community members enjoyed delicious food while spending the morning together outdoors. The sunny weather added to the festive atmosphere as kids and adults alike moved from table to table participating in hands-on cultural activities. There was no shortage of creative outlets for younger attendees. Beach parent Tammy Lee led a hugely popular craft activity where kids made Saja Boys “Gat” hats and Huntrix “Norigae” keychains inspired by K-Pop Demon Hunters. Susan Xu guided students through stencil art, teaching them how to create beautiful designs with Chinese characters, while Betty Rojas and Doris Pira provided coloring sheets and paper lanterns that kept young artists busy throughout the event.

articles.text: Four performances of Grease were on display at Piedmont High School from Thursday to Sunday last week. After the final bow, the cast, crew, and orchestra of Grease stepped away from the spotlight; but not from the work that made the production possible. While audiences saw polished choreography, catchy songs, and confident performances, much of the effort that brought Grease to life happened quietly backstage. For Theo Ferguson, who played Danny Zuko, one of the biggest challenges was navigating the technical side of the show, something audiences rarely notice. “In addition to the memorization and blocking, it’s really important to coordinate with the tech. For example, the microphones are not always working. You have to learn how to project and think on the fly,” Ferguson said. He also emphasized the need to adapt musically, explaining that the band can’t always hear the actors clearly, making flexibility essential. “You have to learn how to adapt to them, not the other way around,” he said. Despite the pressure, the long rehearsal process created a strong sense of community among the cast. During tech week, two weeks of four- to sixhour rehearsals, Ferguson said the support system made all the difference. “When we’re worried about what’s going to happen next or we have to figure out something difficult, it’s always great to look around and just be with a group of good friends and have a laugh Theo Ferguson and Ali Atanasio and the cast of Grease in the Alan Harvey Theater Photos by Marielle Hayes

articles.text: In recent weeks, residents have reported coyote sightings in the Sandringham and St James area. One resident spotted a family of coyotes on their doorstep. Piedmont’s Animal Control has shared safety tips to ensure you’re keeping yourself, your pets, and the coyote safe. Piedmont has a longstanding and stable coyote population. According to Animal Control officer Maria Anwar, February through June is “denning season.” During this time of year, coyotes may become more aggressive to protect their young. They recommend that if you see a coyote, you should keep your distance. Most coyotes fear humans and would prefer to avoid us. If a coyote approaches you, it is recommended that you haze it and scare it away. You can do this by acting big and loud (waving your arms and yelling), making noise with a metal can or whistle, or using tools like a garden hose or spray gun filled with water. Be persistent until the coyote retreats. “Using variety in hazing is important because coyotes learn to recognize and avoid individual people. We recommend changing up hazing tools and methods,” said Officer Anwar. Coyotes can be a threat to pets, especially cats. Officer Anwar recommends that residents walk their pet on a short leash and keep them close. It’s best to bring your pet inside at night. “Coyotes are looking for food. Be cautious about leaving food outside (such as fallen fruit from trees) as this can attract coyotes,” Officer Anwar stated. It is illegal to harm, relocate, or feed coyotes, but if you’d like to safely prevent coyotes from entering your yard, you can follow these tips: • Do not purposely feed animals – animals begin to lose their fear of humans and will continue to return for easy meals. • Clean up possible food resources – pet food, fallen fruits, and secure trash. • Monitor small children and pets while outside, even in a fenced yard. • Install motion-activated lighting and sprinklers • Remove cover and hiding places (thick vegetation, debris piles) – trim plants 2 feet off the ground. articles.text: Biggie is 4-month-old German Shepherd mix Biggie is an adorable and lovable 4-month-old, 43-pound German Shepherd mix who looks like a stuffed animal come to life. He’s a sweet, curious puppy, full of energy and always ready to explore, play, and learn new things. His fosters say he is already showing promise with basic training, including learning “sit” and “stay,” and that he is quickly picking up crate and house training. Biggie thrives when he’s close to his person and is becoming more confident and calm as he settles into his routine. He would do best in an active home where he can get plenty of exercise, mental stimulation, and consistent, positive training. With the right guidance, Biggie is destined to grow into an incredible, loyal companion. articles.text: At almost 14 years old, Gandalf is a confident cat with an affectionate disposition. This mellow tabby is friendly with new people and quick to seek out laps, quiet company, or a cozy spot nearby. His foster calls him the perfect binge-watching and book-reading buddy. Gandalf enjoys some playtime, but can usually be found napping in the sun or living out his dream as a devoted lap cat. Giving him gentle nose rubs may earn you a kiss in return! While he adored cuddles, he’ll do well with an experienced adopter who can read his body language and acknowledge his need for personal space; doing so is richly rewarded with trust and snuggles. This dapper gentleman is positive for Feline Immunodeficiency Virus (FIV), so will need to stay indoors for his own health, and has allergies Adopt Gandalf through Cat Town. that are easily managed with a rabbit-only diet and daily medication that he happily eats mixed into his food. He might do well with another calm cat in the home. Gandalf is neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, FIV-positive, and FeLV-negative. He’s looking for a patient, cat-experienced adopter who’ll go slow and love him for exactly who he is. articles.text: I grew up in Piedmont, walked the halls of Piedmont High School, and learned early what it means to be part of a community that shows up for one another. That sense of support followed me to Boston, where I pursued my undergraduate degree at Boston University (BU) and am now finishing my master’s in public health. While at BU, I had the opportunity to intern with the Grayken Center for Addiction at Boston Medical Center (BMC). Every day, I watched clinicians, researchers, and staff meet patients where they were with dignity, evidence-based care, and an unwavering belief that everyone deserves a chance at better health. The work being done at BMC saves lives, reduces stigma, and helps rebuild communities, but it depends heavily on philanthropy to continue. This April, I’m running the 129th Boston Marathon in support of Boston Medical Center. For me, this race is about far more than 26.2 miles. It’s about honoring the patients I met, the mentors who shaped my education, and the belief that health care should be accessible to all. To run, I’ve committed to raising $10,000 by April 15 to support BMC’s vital programs. I’m asking my hometown community to be part of this journey. Donations of any size truly matter—whether it’s $5 or $500, every contribution helps ensure that patients receive the care they deserve and that future public health professionals can continue this work. Piedmont helped shape who I am today. If you’re able, I would be deeply grateful for your support as I carry that community spirit with me all the way to the Boston Marathon finish line. You can donate by following the link here: https://www.givengain.com/project/eleanor-raising-f unds-for-boston-medical-center-118209 Scan the QR code to support Boston Medical Center at the Boston Marathon 2026.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is hosting a Q&A session to address the community’s questions and concerns over the community pool. The session will be conducted tomorrow, Thursday, February 5, from 5 to 6:30 p.m. at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy, and City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore will host the meeting. They’ll start with a project status recap, then move to a moderated Q&A period. Community members are encouraged to submit questions in advance at piedmont.ca.gov/ PoolQuestion. Questions submitted early will shape the discussion at the event and inform future project communications. This event is intended to give community members direct face time with city leadership and a chance to ask questions and gain a clearer understanding of commissioning before the City takes possession of the community pool. Without an opening date in sight for the community pool, the City intends to increase transparency with the community by releasing project status bulletins at least monthly until the facility opens. articles.text: Piedmont City Council will hold a public hearing Monday, February 2, on proposed Objective Design Standards that would set clear, enforceable rules for how new housing is designed and built in the city. The draft standards are intended to preserve Piedmont’s existing character by ensuring that new housing reflects the scale, proportions, and patterns already present in local neighborhoods. Rather than changing how the city looks, the goal is to make expectations clearer and more predictable. The standards, unanimously recommended by the Planning Commission on January 12, would apply to a wide range of projects, including accessory dwelling units, mixed-use and multifamily housing, new single-family homes, and residential developments of up to four units. City staff and consultants created the standards by converting Piedmont’s existing Design Review Guidelines into Objective Design Standards with clear and measurable criteria. Instead of broad guidance, the rules specify dimensions, placement, and proportions that can be checked for compliance. This approach is intended to provide residents, property owners, and developers with a consistent understanding of what is allowed. For example, the draft regulates architectural elements such as massing and articulation: • Massing refers to a building’s overall size and shape and how its bulk appears from the street. • Articulation describes how a building’s exterior is visually broken up, such as through setbacks, changes in wall planes, or roof forms, to reduce the appearance of large, box-like structures. Community feedback also influenced the proposal. Input from two public open houses, an online survey, and two Planning Commission study sessions informed several provisions, including rules governing driveway design and window placement, reflecting common concerns about safety and privacy. The City Council meeting will take place during its regular session Monday evening. Learn more about this initiative and see materials and video from previous discussions at piedmont.ca.gov/ObjectiveDesignStandards. articles.text: On February 3, Piedmont’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee will receive a presentation outlining a variety of potential funding mechanisms related to new housing development and affordable housing, including impact fees, community facilities districts, and modifications to the City’s municipal services parcel tax. After the presentation, the Committee will consider recommending that the City Council authorize further study of these funding mechanisms and how they might work in Piedmont. This presentation is part of the City’s ongoing work to implement the 2023 Housing Element, which committed to such a review. The Committee’s recommendations will be discussed at Planning Commission and City Council meetings in the coming months. A final decision to pursue and fund a detailed study of any of these potential programs would be made by the City Council. Email comments to the Committee can be sent to the staff liaison, Finance Director Kiran Bawa at kbawa@piedmont. ca.gov. The presentation will address these concepts: • Development impact fees: one-time fees on new housing development used to help fund public infrastructure. • Mello-Roos Community Facilities District: a “special tax” for a defined geographic area used to fund public infrastructure and services. • Municipal Services Parcel Tax: considering a new rate category for 2-4 unit structures (Townhome/Multifamily). • Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee: would allow developers of multi-family housing to pay a one-time fee instead of providing affordable units on-site, if the City were to adopt inclusionary requirements. • Affordable Housing Fund: create a fund in the City’s budget to receive and manage in-lieu fees, donations, and other sources of funding for affordable housing. articles.text: As PHS seniors enter the second semester, labels like “second-semester senior” and “senioritis” are often used to describe changes in motivation and workload. However, for many students, this period is not about laziness. It is a deserved exhale after months, and sometimes years, of intense effort. The first semester of senior year is dominated by college applications, deadlines, and the constant need to perform. By second semester, much of that intensity fades. “I feel like this semester is a lot more stress-free compared to last semester because college apps are over,” Dimitri Secor said, describing this time as a chance to simply “flow through classes.” Jameson Sanford echoed that change, noting that teachers seem to recognize it as well. “I think teachers are being more mindful about the amount of work they’re giving out this semester because they know a lot of kids are waiting to hear back from colleges,” Sanford said. Despite the uncertainty of decisions, she described the semester as feeling “lighter in the sense that I’m almost out of high school.” That lighter academic load has also transformed the social atmosphere on campus. “The energy on campus among seniors feels a lot more connected and more stress-free,” Mira Sachs said. “We can just enjoy learning and spending time with each other.” Still, a slower pace does not erase the effort seniors invested earlier in the year. Some students deliberately shifted their workload to second semester after prioritizing applications. Petro Papahadjopoulos chose to take more challenging classes after months of writing and revising. “I applied to so many colleges and I was doing work for seven months,” he said. “I’m really glad that I have more free time and I can just do homework instead of having to think about supplementals.” As academic pressure eases, another factor emerges, one unique to second-semester senior year. For the first time, the end of high school feels immediate. Ordinary moments begin to feel finite, and routines seniors once rushed through take on new meaning. This emotional awareness, absent from any other period of high school, shapes how students experience their final months. “I feel really sad that it’s about to end soon,” Donovan Sar-Garza said. “I’m trying to make a lot of memories.” Rather than dismissing seniors as unmotivated, second semester of senior year should be recognized as a moment of earned rest and reflection. After years of balancing academics, extracurriculars, and college applications, seniors deserve the space to slow down, reconnect, and fully experience the closing chapter of their high school lives. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern reporter for the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: Scouting has been incredibly rewarding for our family—for my daughter, Abby, because every moment feels like an adventure, and for me, because I get to watch her grow into a confident, capable, and self-reliant young person. Our journey began in Cub Scouts when Abby was in second grade. For a child who loves hiking, exploring forests, making friends, and learning by doing, Scouting opened a world of possibilities. Abby is very much a “live in the moment” kid, and Scouting meets her exactly where she is. Whether she’s hiking at Point Reyes, shooting rockets and sliding down sand dunes at Dillon Beach, or backpacking 25 miles through Desolation Wilderness with her all-girls group—nicknamed “The Chipmunks”— she relishes every adventure. Through merit badges, she’s also been introduced to a wide range of skills, hobbies, and even possible career paths. One of the most meaningful parts of Scouting is the community. Abby is a unique kid, like so many others, and her troop celebrates that individuality. articles.text: Do you remember the first time your child saw bubbles? That moment when a shimmering sphere floated past their face, and their eyes went wide, their whole body stilled? We’ve all had that thought: I wish I could feel that kind of wonder again. Here’s the thing: you can. What’s captivating about bubbles isn’t childish—it’s profound. Bubbles are tiny physics laboratories floating through the air, demonstrating principles that fascinate kids, scientists, and artists alike. The wonder doesn’t disappear as we grow; we just stop paying attention. The beauty of bubbles is their accessibility. You don’t need special equipment or expertise. In a world of enrichment programs, optimized activities, and overscheduled weekends, there’s something radical about slowing down with something simple. Bubbles have captivated visitors at the Exploratorium since 1969—our bubble stations and Soap Film Painting exhibit remain among our most beloved. But these aren’t experiences that only happen on a museum floor. They happen in your kitchen with ingredients you already have. Maybe your kids are still young, and bubbles remain a regular source of entertainment. Maybe they’ve grown, and it’s been years since bubbles were part of your routine. Either way, bubbles offer something rare: permission to pause and really look. When you do, there’s so much to notice. Why are bubbles always spheres? Why those shifting rainbow colors? Why do they last longer on humid days? You don’t need to know the answers—surface tension, light interference, evaporation—to explore together. The questions are the point. For a simple but deeper dive, try this: create a bubble solution, pour it into a shallow pan, and use a straw to blow bubbles on the surface of the pan. Start with one. How big a bubble can you blow? What happens when you blow two bubbles next to each other? Can you add a third? How might you blow a bubble inside another bubble? When my daughters were little, we’d spend countless afternoons testing bubble theories. Now they’re teenagers, but bubbles still catch our attention from time to time, not from nostalgia, but because there’s still more to notice. Just the other day as our dog jumped into the air to snap at a bubble floating by her nose, we wondered together if different bubbles smell different from one another and what kinds of bubbles smell best. That’s the secret about wonder: it doesn’t require complexity. Sometimes the most meaningful moments come from the simplest things. So skip the elaborate activity this weekend. Dig out that bottle of soap. Chase bubbles. Have conversations. And let yourself be amazed again. The science is there, waiting in every shimmering sphere—but so is something more fundamental. The pure, uncomplicated joy your child knew all along. The reminder that less really can be more. For complete instructions on this bubble activity, visit the Exploratorium’s Watch and Do Science collection at exploratorium.edu/education/ifi/watchand-do Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team finished the last week with a win and loss against two Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division opponents. They beat Encinal at Witter Field 2-nil on Wednesday, January 28, but lost 2-1 to Berkeley at the Yellowjackets’ home field on Friday, January 30. The pair of results brings the Highlanders’ record to 7-2-5 (W-T-L) and 2-1-3 against league opponents with four matches left in the regular season. “Against Encinal, it may have been the first time the girls have experienced a low block. Early on we struggled, In the second-half we spoke about ball-speed and moving it quickly. Berkeley plays a 4-3-3 and leaves three players really high,” explained coach Matt Spencer-Harty. Piedmont is currently the North Coast Section’s No. 22 ranked school by Maxpreps, which puts them on track for a Division 2 berth. “Our team is really connecting together. We need to keep working on our mindset going into playoffs and important games. Our speed of play against Encinal wasn’t it’s best, but our defense is playing well,” junior Chloe Toyama said. Against Encinal, Piedmont dominated possession, but went into halftime in a 0-0 tie. They quickly scored in the 46th minute on a corner kick, where Arden Sorensen-Wald lifted a pass to the center of the box for Stephanie Lee to score. Piedmont’s final goal came in the 60th minute by Ayla Blanford when Liu turned a defender inside-out with a slick touch, finding Blanford storming into the box. “It was a great ball from the midfield into Miranda. Working off of her and seeing how we can find back-space has been really helpful,” Blanford said. Fullback Chloe Toyama looks to make a play on a corner kick against Encinal. side, taking a shot on her first touch to the far post for a goal. 2-1 loss to Berkeley Berkeley struck quickly in the third minute of action long shot from about eight yards above the penalty area. The Yellowjackets made it 2-nil just 10 minutes later in the 13th when a long pass was played down the right side, leading to Berkeley’s right winger making a few dribbles into the box before slotting in a shot on a 1-on-1 situation with the PHS goalie. articles.text: Piedmont suffered a 2-1 loss to Hayward, its sixth straight loss. Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team suffered a 2-1 loss on the road at Hayward High on Thursday, January 29. The result marked the Highlanders’ sixth loss in a row. Piedmont has three matches left in the regular season: Berkeley on February 6, Bishop O’Dowd on February 10, and Castro Valley on February 12. Against Hayward, Piedmont struck first in the 11th minute following a giveaway in the Farmers’ own box when Roman Ahearn was well-placed to jump on an errant pass—curling a left-footed shot above the keeper. Hayward found the equalizer in the 44th minute, eventually going ahead in the final minutes of the game. 2-1 loss to Hayward Piedmont scored the game’s first goal in the 11th minute. It started when Eli Dao-Hoang chipped a ball across the face of the goal. When a Hayward defender looked to play a pass out, he sloppily turned the ball over to Ahearn within their own penalty area. Ahearn took one touch with his right foot to center the ball to himself and followed through with his left to perfectly place his shot above the keeper. Matias Seelenberger also nearly scored on a shot from 12 yards above the penalty area in the 16th minute, but it was pushed wide for a corner. Four minutes into the half Hayward got the equalizer. It happened after PHS suffered a giveaway in the back, where the Farmers’ striker won possession off a center back, nicking the ball Staff Photos out wide to their left winger. The Hayward forward took one touch around a defender before slotting in his shot. Hayward’s game-winner came in the final 10 minutes of action on a second goal by the Farmers’ Yurem Alberto. Piedmont had no more shots on target in the remaining 40 minutes of action. They had one chance from a corner, where a pass in from the right side found Elias Reed-Miguel, but his attempt on the volley sailed high over the net. Tuesday vs. Alameda Piedmont hosted Alameda on Tuesday, February 3. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-0-12 overall, 0-3 league) hosts Berkeley on Friday, February 6 at 6:30 p.m. Roman Ahearn scored for Piedmont in the 11th minute. articles.text: In a shocking end to the boys’ basketball game between Piedmont High and the visiting San Leandro Pirates, a brawl spilled out onto the court that made the KTVU news. Piedmont High principal David Yoshihara issued the following statement on the matter: “We are reaching out to you tonight with a heavy heart following the disturbing events that transpired at the conclusion of the boys varsity basketball game against San Leandro High School. For those of you who were in attendance, we recognize that what you witnessed was both shocking and deeply upsetting… Our primary concern is the well-being of our community. We want to confirm that all Piedmont High School players and coaching staff are safe and no Piedmont High School players were physically harmed during the altercation. However, we are deeply saddened to report that several staff members and students sustained injuries during the altercation. These individuals were treated by on-site medical personnel and and we are incredibly grateful to the staff and bystanders who acted quickly to protect others. Seeing a community event turn into a scene of conflict is a traumatic experience for students and parents alike. We want to ensure that those who were present have the support they need: • Processing the Event: It is normal to feel anxious or upset after witnessing such an incident. We encourage you to talk with your children about what they saw. • Counseling/Wellness Resources: The high school counseling office and wellness center will be open and available for students starting Monday morning to provide a safe space to process these events. The Piedmont High School administration is working in full cooperation with the Piedmont Police Department, San Leandro High School leadership, and WACC/NCS. A comprehensive investigation is underway to identify those involved and ensure full accountability. Violence has no place in our schools or at our athletic events. We are currently reviewing our security protocols for all future home games to ensure that our gym remains a space where families can gather safely. We want to thank the many parents and community members who remained calm and helped lead students, fans, and players to safety during the chaos. Your composure in a difficult moment reflected the true spirit of Piedmont. We will provide further updates as more information becomes available. In the meantime, please do not hesitate to reach out to the administration if you have specific concerns or information that may assist in the investigation. With concern and care. – David Yoshihara.” At the final whistle, video shows three San Leandro High players approach Piedmont High’s student section to gloat its win. Per video of the event, as well as multiple people in attendance, Piedmont’s students came off the bleachers to confront the SLHS players. After one Piedmont student bumped chests with a San Leandro player, mayhem ensued. Per video of the incident, a San Leandro player shoved the PHS student in response, and then Piedmont students shoved back. SLHS’s bench rushed over, and one of their players slugged a Piedmont student. Piedmont athletic director Tyler Small attempted to get in the middle to separate the two sides. Small was visibly holding back three San Leandro players, including one who was squaring up to throw punches. Then, San Leandro head coach Davion Berry locked Small’s forearm under his armpit, and then either a San Leandro assistant coach or parent threw Small to the ground from behind. Berry and SL players then jumped on the athletic director on the ground with one player visibly throwing punches. Berry had to be held back even after Small rose from the ground. In more video obtained by The Post, San Leandro coaches and parents cornered a referee as he looked to exit the gym. As a response, Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team announced that Wednesday, February 4’s game against Bishop O’Dowd will be played without any spectators. Neither of Piedmont High’s players nor coaches was ever involved.

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California [OMCA] will host its 25th Annual Lunar New Year festival on February 21, offering a range of family-friendly art and cultural activities celebrating the Year of the Horse. The museum’s annual event connects Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) heritage to the greater Bay Area community with a full day of cultural performances, family-friendly storytelling, hands-on activities, delicious food from local AAPI chefs and opportunities to support local AAPI artisans. The festival begins with a “Lucky lion dance” performed by LionDanceME, a team of internationally-recognized performers. LionDanceME was founded in 2013 by San Francisco resident Norman Lau and a group of San Francisco Unified School District students. The group regularly performs at OMCA’s Lunar New Year celebrations. OMCA will also host Oakland-based Japanese-American artist Seiji Oda, whose signature ambient “lo-fi” and hyphy sound will fill the garden alongside several other performances spanning Korean, Pilipino, Vietnamese, and Chinese traditions. An energetic performance by UC Berkeley’s Vietnamese Student Association Lion and Dragon Dance Team for good luck and prosperity in the New Year closes out the festival at 3:30 p.m. activities and visit https://museumca.org/event/25th-annual-lunar-new-year-at-omca-year-ofthe-horse/ for more information.

articles.text: The historic “Spreckles Organ” was commissioned by philanthropist John Spreckles and is designed to blend into the museum’s structure. Visit Legion of Honor in San Francisco any Saturday afternoon at 4 p.m. and enjoy a free organ concert in the Rodin Gallery by local classically trained organists Jonathan Dimmock, Joy-Leilani Garbutt or Christopher Keady. Dimmock is a graduate of Oberlin and Yale, and the first American to hold the prestigious position of organ scholar of Westminster Abbey. He was resident organist at St. John the Divine in New York City, St. Mark’s in Minneapolis, and Grace Cathedral in San Francisco. Dimmock is principal organist at the Legion of Honor, organist for the San Francisco Symphony, and director of music at Congregation Sherith Israel. He has recorded a Grammy-winning record with the San Francisco Symphony. Garbutt is an organist and cofounder of the Boulanger Initiative, a nonprofit organization that supports female composers. Garbutt spent a year in France researching early 20th-century organ music by female composers exclusively, and currently serves as the director of music for St. Luke’s Episcopal Church in San Francisco. Keady is the interim director of music at the famous Grace Cathedral in San Francisco, where he serves as principal accompanist for the Cathedral Choir of Men and Boys and performs on the cathedral’s Alexander Memorial Organ. Concerts begin at 4 p.m. in Gallery 10 and are free to all museum patrons. All concerts feature the museum’s historic 1924 Skinner pipe organ, called the “Spreckels Organ,” and last approximately 45 minutes to one hour. The concerts are part of the museum’s ongoing dedication to art and music, often featuring a diverse repertoire that complements the surrounding sculptures. The historic “Spreckles Organ” was commissioned by philanthropist John Spreckles and is designed to blend into the museum’s structure. Its 4,500 pipes are not outwardly visible, and the ceiling of the gallery is canvas so that the organ can be heard throughout the gallery and museum. The canvas ceiling is painted as a trompe-l’œil to resemble a marble apse. Residents of all nine Bay Area counties, including Alameda, receive free admission to Legion of Honor in San Francisco on Saturdays. Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Solano, and Sonoma residents can visit the museum during operating hours and view any of its permanent collection galleries. Visitors ages 17 and under always receive free admission to the permanent collection galleries. Visit https://www.famsf.org/ events/organ-concert to learn more and to register.

articles.text: Cal Performances at UC Berkeley will present mezzo-soprano Joyce DiDonato with the genre-crossing string trio Time for Three in Emily – No Prisoner Be, a new, evening-length song cycle by Pulitzer Prize–winning composer Kevin Puts, on Saturday, February 7 at 8 p.m. in Zellerbach Hall. The new work sets 24 poems by Emily Dickinson to composer Kevin Puts’ score, featuring stage lighting design from Andrew Staples that the creators say “magnifies the emotional terrain of Dickinson’s language.” Mezzo-soprano Joyce DiDonato, making her return to the Bay Area following acclaimed projects including Eden (2023) and In War & Peace: Harmony Through Music (2016), leads the program vocally. Each member of Time for Three, including Nicolas Kendall (viola, violin), Charles Yang (violin) and Ranaan Meyer (bass), will perform alongside DiDonato. Time for Three won a Grammy in 2023 for their recording of Puts’s triple concerto Contact. Emily – No Prisoner Be marks DiDonato’s first appearance with Cal Performances in this collaboration and continues her long creative partnership with Puts.She previously performed a lead role in his opera The Hours. A studio recording of Emily – No Prisoner Be is scheduled for release on January 30, with four tracks already available on streaming platforms: “Because I could not stop for Death —,” “There is another sky,” “Her Face,” and “They shut me up.” The project reflects DiDonato’s advocacy for making music broadly accessible. articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) is marking its 20th anniversary with Continuum: MoAD Over Time, an exhibition examining the museum’s history, on view now through March 1. Continuum presents a chronological and thematic overview of MoAD’s development from its founding to the present, while also addressing its future direction. The exhibition features archival materials, fine art, interviews and community narratives that document the museum’s impact on arts education, cultural programming and public engagement, as well as its artistic influence in the Bay Area and beyond. Exhibition highlights include materials related to long-running initiatives such as the museum’s Emerging Artist Program and “MoAD in the Classroom,” as well as community events including the Afropolitan Ball and Diaspora Dinner. These elements illustrate how the institution has supported artists of the African Diaspora and expanded access to cultural resources over two decades. Photo courtesy of Museum of the African Diaspora Chester Higgins’s “The Girl from Ghana” viewed from outside the Museum of the African Diaspora. Continuum includes works by Cheryl Patrice Derricotte, Chester Higgins Jr., JoeSam., Richard Mayhew, Ramekon O’Arwisters, Gordon Parks, Lava Thomas and Sam Vernon. These artists’ contributions reflect a range of media and perspectives connected to the museum’s mission. According to MoAD, Continuum is intended to document the organization’s institutional history while providing context for its next phase of growth. The exhibition is supported by the KHR McNeely Family Foundation, with major funding from the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, CommonSpirit Health and San Francisco Grants for the Arts. Additional support is provided by several foundations, corporations and individual donors, including the Richard Mayhew Exhibition Fund. Continuum: MoAD Over Time is now on view at the Museum of the African Diaspora. For more information, visit https://www. moadsf.org.

articles.text: Most people wonder what happens after they die. Do they progress to some form of afterlife, simply cease to exist, or encounter something stranger altogether? The Good Place builds an entire comedy around that uncertainty. Created and produced by Michael Schur, the creative force behind The Office and Parks and Recreation, the series follows four people who have died and end up in a version of heaven known as the “Good Place.” They arrive because they supposedly lived their lives well enough to meet the required criteria. The Good Place itself is presented as a perfect dream, where everything goes according to plan, benefits its inhabitants, and even assigns perfectly matched soulmates. For any given person, including our characters, entry into the Good Place depends on an extremely high count of moral points earned by positively impacting the universe over the course of a lifetime. Each action carries a positive or negative value, and at the end of a person’s life, those points are tallied to determine their place in the afterlife. Those who fall short are sent to the “Bad Place.” At least, that’s how things are explained to Eleanor Shellstrop (Kristen Bell) by Michael (Ted Danson), the architect of the Good Place, when she wakes up in his office-like room after Kristen Bell, William Jackson Harper, Ted Danson and D’Arcy Carden star in The Good Place being run over by shopping carts while picking up margarita mix. Michael introduces Eleanor to Chidi (William Jackson Harper), a former professor of moral philosophy and the person “the system” has chosen as her soulmate. Eleanor also meets Tahani (Jameela Jamil), a British socialite and prolific philanthropist, and Jianyu (Manny Jacinto), a silent Taiwanese Buddhist monk. They would be perfect neighbors for Eleanor, a death-row lawyer and humanitarian, as Michael repeatedly describes her, because they have all supposedly earned their places through the good lives they led on Earth. The problem is that Eleanor is not who Michael believes she is. In her own words, she’s an “Arizona dirtbag” who made a living selling fake medication to the elderly, even earning the title of top employee five years in a row. From that moment on, the series becomes less about the afterlife itself and more about whether people can meaningfully change. Unsurprisingly, Eleanor’s perfect afterlife house turns out to be her nightmare, filled with clown pictures and minimalist Scandinavian design, clearly meant for a very different Eleanor Shellstrop. Faced with the fact that she is in the Good Place by mistake, Eleanor tries to keep her secret and avoid being sent to the Bad Place. She confides in Chidi, who agrees to help her become a better person by teaching her ethics. It doesn’t come easily. He portrays – he inhabits –the character Paul Hunham, a classics teacher at a New England boarding school. The year is 1970. He is considered, by students and faculty, to be a dedicated curmudgeon who long ago abandoned his conviction that he could make a difference in the lives of his students, whom he calls “troglodytes” and “smarmy Visigoths.” There is a sadness to the delight he seems to take in dropping graded blue book exams on their desks, most with large Fs and Ds. The narrative begins in earnest when Paul is called to the office of the headmaster and is told that the Christmas holiday is approaching and during this two week hiatus four students, who for various reasons, must remain at the school. articles.text: Secretariat is a Disney film about a magnificent chestnut racehorse Secretariat, nicknamed Big Red, considered by many as the greatest racehorse of all time. In 1973 against all odds he won the Triple Crown: the Kentucky Derby, the Preakness and the Belmont Stakes. articles.text: On a cool, mild midwinter morning last Wednesday, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group set out once again, this time with a strong turnout of 47 walkers and four canine companions. The destination was one of Piedmont’s least understood landmarks: the EBMUD “Reservoir Number Two,” tucked near the top of Blair Avenue. The walk combined a steady uphill climb with a deep dive into local history. The group gathered at the Exedra before winding through Highland, Sierra, Sheridan and Lakeview avenues, then up Poplar Way. From Mountain Avenue, walkers began the steeper ascent along Bellevue, Pacific and Hager avenues toward Blair. Just down the street, behind a fence and largely hidden from view, sat the massive, long-decommissioned reservoir. The group paused there for a story-filled stop and a group photo. This was not the first Walking on Wednesdays visit to the site. The group last stopped there in 2024, but interest has grown following earlier discussions of Deep Oakland, a book by Andrews Alden. Two years ago, walkers Karin Fetherston and Peggy Shultz introduced the group to Alden’s work, which explores how geology shaped Oakland and the East Bay, including a chapter on Piedmont. Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website, historyofpiedmont.com, also provides extensive background and historical photos of the reservoir. Alden explains that Piedmont sits atop a rare geological feature known as the “Piedmont block,” a separate chunk of the Earth’s crust west of the Hayward Fault. Roughly four miles by two miles in size, this rocky block neatly encloses the city and reaches about half the elevation of the high Oakland hills. The eastern edge aligns with the Hayward Fault, which runs along the Montclair district. Oakland was incorporated in 1852, fueled by Gold Rush–era growth. The city developed near the Bay on land dominated by oak forests growing atop ancient sand dunes. Early infrastructure struggled with loose soils, prompting city leaders in the 1860s to pave streets with crushed stone. Much of that stone came from quarries embedded in the Piedmont block. All of the block’s rocks belong to the Franciscan Complex, a massive and geologically diverse formation found throughout California’s Coast Range. Beneath Piedmont lies hard, thick-bedded sandstone that was heavily quarried in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and used widely across the East Bay. The Piedmont block’s gentler slopes differ from the steeper hills east of the Hayward Fault. Its rocky rims form a natural watershed, forcing moist Bay air upward where it cools and condenses into fog and rain. As a result, the area receives more rainfall than surrounding lowlands and supports five permanent creeks that eventually converge at Lake Merritt. Water access shaped early settlement. Small East Bay towns initially relied on household wells, followed by private water companies that offered more dependable service. Providers with access to higher ground had a major advantage: gravity-fed systems that delivered steady pressure without pumps. William Dingee, born in Pennsylvania in 1854, arrived in Oakland in 1877 and found success in real estate. In 1891, he sought to supply water to Piedmont’s growing residential areas. When the Contra Costa Water Company declined his request, Dingee moved forward on his own, boring 22 tunnels into the Oakland hills to tap groundwater from springs. Though limited, the water could flow downhill to a reservoir without pumps. By 1893, Dingee was operating the Piedmont Springs and Water Company, piping water from Moraga Peak to a reservoir in Piedmont. That reservoir provided gravity-fed pressure to surrounding neighborhoods. Originally an open basin, it was later covered with a concrete and steel lid. Dingee soon became Contra Costa’s main competitor, triggering price wars and bitter disputes. The companies merged around the turn of the century, with Dingee placed in charge, but the arrangement did not last. In 1906, the Peoples Water Company, led by Frank C. Havens, absorbed Contra Costa and other providers. Dingee’s finances collapsed soon after, and he spent his remaining years in obscurity in Sacramento, dying in 1941. As demand continued to grow, Peoples Water was absorbed into the East Bay Water Company in 1916. By 1919, ten East Bay reservoirs, including those in Piedmont, were used for filtration or sterilization. Public sentiment shifted toward public ownership, leading voters to approve the creation of EBMUD in 1923. Reservoir Number Two occupies more than nine acres along the Oakland-Piedmont border, with 8.3 acres in Piedmont. articles.text: Looking around at the many kennel clubs and private dog trainers offering classes, you are likely to notice the AKC Canine Good Citizenship Test being offered- A LOT. A typical class will be held weekly and offer the opportunity to test during the final class with an approved AKC Evaluator. According to the American Kennel Club website, “Canine Good Citizen is a 10-skill test that teaches good manners to dogs and responsible dog ownership to their owners.” In summary, it’s your chance to show off your dog’s basic obedience skills and earn a title (and maybe a ribbon!). So why train for the CGC Test? For most, it is not simply about titles or ribbons. The ten skills highlighted in the test mark the basic skills necessary for a dog to be considered polite in public settings. While these skills are not hard to teach, it is painfully obvious when a dog has not yet met this benchmark. Taking the test can be a simple way to celebrate having a dog who is reliable and well mannered, as well as the effort it took to get there. The ten items on the test are: 1. Accepting a friendly stranger 2. Sitting politely for petting 3. Demonstrating your dog is comfortable being handled and brushed 4. Walking your dog on a loose leash showing right, left, and about turns, plus stop. 5. Walking through a crowd 6. Sit and down on command/ staying in place 7. Coming when called 8. Reacting politely to another dog 9. Reacting appropriately to distractions (no excessive fear or aggression) 10. Handler goes out of sight for 3-minutes and the dog remains quiet and calm with a volunteer. Many organizations that work with dogs may require the CGC test as part of their training program. For example, most therapy dogs must pass the basic CGC test, and service dogs complete all three levels (CGC, CGCA, CGCU) for public access testing. It is important to remember that passing the CGC test does not give any dog, even service dogs in training, full public access by law (only completion of service dog training does this). Even if these working dog professions are not for you, the training to prepare for the CGC test is fun and rewarding. Mastering these basic skills opens the door for more advanced training and will likely reduce stress when bringing your canine companion into public settings. Whether you train at home or participate in a preparatory class, the AKC Canine Good Citizenship Test is quickly becoming the modern standard for basic obedience. So what are you waiting for? Pick up a leash and jump into training! Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507–2017, email Sierra109@gmail.com, or visit her website at www.oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com. articles.text: On a quiet stretch of Mountain Boulevard in Montclair, the scent of butter, citrus, and sugar drifts out of Full Belly Bakery, pulling in neighbors on morning walks, parents ducking in after school drop-off, and customers who swear they’re “not really cake people.” Inside, owner Eva Allen is doing what she’s been doing for years now: turning carefully balanced flavors into cakes that feel celebratory without being cloyingly-sweet. Allen didn’t set out to open a storefront. After graduating from Loyola University New Orleans in 2016, she worked in the hospitality industry and baked at home as a creative outlet. What began as something to decompress after work quickly turned into something more. Friends encouraged her to sell what she was making, and in New Orleans, where cottage baking laws made it easy, she began taking orders on the side. When Allen returned to the Bay Area, Full Belly Bakery came with her. She balanced baking with coaching gymnastics and then weathered the uncertainty of the pandemic. While many bakeries shut down, demand for custom cakes surged. Full Belly grew fast, operating first out of Allen’s mom’s house and then a series of commissary kitchens. The arrangement kept costs down but made production difficult, Allen said, especially when it came to storing hundreds of pounds of flour, sugar, and butter. to stop hopping from kitchen to kitchen. She signed a lease on a former Subway space in Montclair and spent seven months navigating permits, inspections, and build-out delays. When Full Belly Bakery finally opened its doors in October 2023, the response was overwhelming. Customers lined up before opening, and by nightfall, nearly everything had sold out. “We went through what we had prepped for the whole weekend in one day,” Allen recalls. Two years in, the bakery is still finding its rhythm. Foot traffic ebbs and flows: slower during the week, busier on Saturdays, and bustling on Sundays thanks to the nearby Montclair Farmers Market. While Full Belly doesn’t have a market booth, Allen occasionally sends staff over during holidays to spread the word. “It’s a way to remind people we’re here,” she says. In Montclair, Full Belly stands alongside just one other nearby bakery, Miette, with even Safeway sending customers across the street over for custom cakes. Cakes are the bakery’s backbone – birthday cakes, wedding cakes, and custom designs, all decorated in buttercream rather than fondant. Fondant, Allen says, is labor-intensive and often more about appearance than taste. Buttercream aligns better with her philosophy: desserts that are nuanced and never overwhelmingly sweet. “I hate grocery store cakes,” Allen says bluntly. “They’re just too sweet.” Many customers who claim they don’t like cake, she’s found, feel the same way. Full Belly’s desserts aim to change that. Wedding clients frequently report that they underestimated how much cake they’d need “because people actually ate it,” she said. That approach carries through the menu. Alongside familiar flavors like chocolate, vanilla, carrot cake, and tiramisu are rotating seasonal offerings: blood orange pistachio, lavender lemon, banana cake with chocolate peanut butter, and a summer favorite: coconut cake with slow-roasted balsamic strawberries and pasFull Belly Bakery storefront Eva Allen, owner of Full Belly Bakery in Montclair. sion fruit curd. “Customers often start with traditional flavors like chocolate and vanilla, then branch out to [our seasonal flavors] once they realize how good it is,” Allen said. Behind the scenes, Full Belly operates on multiple fronts. Retail sales anchor the storefront, while wholesale partnerships with Berkeley Bowl, Piedmont Grocery, Village Market, and others provide stability. Wholesale is more predictable, Allen said, but cash flow can be tight when orders and payments are delayed. “It’s one of the hardest parts of running a small business,” she said. Still, wholesale is where she sees growth. Allen is actively pitching local grocery stores across the East Bay and San Francisco, learning sales skills on the fly. Some of Full Belly’s earliest wholesale opportunities came from chance, through an Instagram message or a customer who loved a particular cake. Now Allen spends time out of the bakery, making connections while her employees keep production running. The bakery’s small team reflects its scrappy, communal beginnings. At the chaotic grand opening, friends and family jumped in to help. One employee, now a regular fixture, was hired on the spot after his mom volunteered him mid-rush. For Allen, the bakery has always been about more than cake. It’s about creating something local, and welcoming, whether that’s donating excess desserts when possible, experimenting with naturally gluten-free treats made without additives, or helping a neighborhood celebrate milestones, big and small. “People are still finding out that we’re here,” Allen says. But in Montclair, word travels fast — especially when it smells this good.

By Sierra Berrick Looking around at the many kennel clubs and private dog trainers offering classes, you are likely to notice the AKC Canine Good Citizenship Test being offered- A LOT. A typical class will be held weekly and offer the opportunity to test during the final class with an approved AKC Evaluator. According to the American Kennel Club website, “Canine Good Citizen is a 10-skill test that teaches good manners to dogs and responsible dog ownership to their owners.” In summary, it’s your chance to show off your dog’s basic obedience skills and earn a title (and maybe a ribbon!). So why train for the CGC Test? For most, it is not simply about titles or ribbons. The ten skills highlighted in the test mark the basic skills necessary for a dog to be considered polite in public settings. While these skills are not hard to teach, it is painfully obvious when a dog has not yet met this benchmark. Taking the test can be a simple way to celebrate having a dog who is reliable and well mannered, as well as the effort it took to get there. The ten items on the test are: 1. Accepting a friendly stranger 2. Sitting politely for petting 3. Demonstrating your dog is comfortable being handled and brushed 4. Walking your dog on a loose leash showing right, left, and about turns, plus stop. 5. Walking through a crowd 6. Sit and down on command/ staying in place 7. Coming when called 8. Reacting politely to another dog 9. Reacting appropriately to distractions (no excessive fear or aggression) 10. Handler goes out of sight for 3-minutes and the dog remains quiet and calm with a volunteer. Many organizations that work with dogs may require the CGC test as part of their training program. For example, most therapy dogs must pass the basic CGC test, and service dogs complete all three levels (CGC, CGCA, CGCU) for public access testing. It is important to remember that passing the CGC test does not give any dog, even service dogs in training, full public access by law (only completion of service dog training does this). Even if these working dog professions are not for you, the training to prepare for the CGC test is fun and rewarding. Mastering these basic skills opens the door for more advanced training and will likely reduce stress when bringing your canine companion into public settings. Whether you train at home or participate in a preparatory class, the AKC Canine Good Citizenship Test is quickly becoming the modern standard for basic obedience. So what are you waiting for? articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The Flix Fest’s February feature is Lost in Translation, directed by Sofia Coppola. The film won critical acclaim in addition to the Original Screenplay Oscar; the movie was also nominated for Best Film, Best Director, and Best Actor, Murray’s first solo nomination in his film career. The 2003 film balances humor and subtle pathos in a moving, melancholy story of an aging movie star named Bob Harris (Bill Murray) and a conflicted newlywed, Charlotte (Scarlett Johansson), who meet in the neon-drenched backdrop of Tokyo’s alien landscape. Strangers in a foreign land, the two find escape, distraction, and understanding after a chance meeting in a quiet lull of their hotel bar. Coppola’s screenplay combines a minimal script with facial expressions, body language, and strategic silences to create an intimacy between Bob and Charlotte that grows during their time together in Tokyo. It will be screened on Thursday, February 12, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45 p.m, and the movie is free to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis and are free to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie is 400 Blows, a 1959 French crime drama by Francois Truffaut, to be shown on March 12, 2026.

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School Over the MLK weekend the Troop 4 Piedmont Scouts went camping in Yosemite Valley. The first day we arrived we had a picnic on the snowy Cathedral Beach on the Merced River close to El Capitan. We had lunch and lively snowball fights. Later we went to set up the tents in the campsite at Upper Pines. A few of the senior patrol leaders helped us do lashings. We tied wood dowel tripods with rope to use as light stands later in the dark. This was a very useful tool we used both nights and satisfied a requirement for the 1st class Scout rank. Dinner followed, spaghetti cooked over the camp stove and - of course - s’mores, over a blazing campfire. It was a cold first night. The temperature dropped from 50F during the day to 25F during the night. We managed to stay warm near the blazing fire, snuggled up in many layers of jackets and later in our warm sleeping bags in the tents. On the second day, Troop 4 started early with a tasty breakfast of eggs and bacon which gave us energy for hiking. Some of us in the group went to the top of Yosemite Falls while the others went to the Lower Falls. The hike to the falls is a climbing rocky trail surrounded by tall evergreen trees and massive granite walls. Yosemite Falls is an impressive waterfall, the tallest in North America (2425 ft). There are 66 steep switchbacks on the way (we counted). We admired a beautiful giant rainbow in the mist of the powerful waterflow while eating Violet (left), Alexa, Winnie, Aria, and Lorea cook a meal at the Upper Pines campsite Blake (front), Colin and Nico cook breakfast Troop 4 Piedmont Scouts in Yosemite Valley with Half Dome in the background a tasty lunch of bagels and cream cheese. At the top the view of the valley was splendid, and the sound of the waterfall was roaring. The 3rd group of scouts hiked in the valley by the Merced River using the map and compass to guide their way to the base of El Capitan. El Capitan is a famous monolith, known for its vertical granite walls, about 3,000 feet high, and a challenge for many skilled rock climbers. We looked through binoculars to spot some of the climbers who appeared like tiny specs from a distance. After hiking the scouts had a delicious dinner of ramen at the campsite, (and s’mores by the fire again). Then we went Ice Skating in the pitch-black night. At the glowing white ice-skating rink with lively music playing in the background, we bonded with some new friends from Troop 320. We had a lot of good laughs as we were awkwardly sliding and falling across the slippery ice. Scouts who were not ice skating were cheering on the passing ice skaters and offering hi-fives at each lap. A bonfire outside the rink kept warm those waiting for the ice skaters. On the last day we all drove home, singing and laughing on the car ride. After the 4-hour drive, Troop 4 came back to beautiful sunny bay area weather. We were happy and satisfied to be home after a memorable weekend full of adventure in Yosemite. We had spent time outside in the fresh air surrounded by beautiful mountains, nature and breath-taking views in the company of good friends. A little preparation now can save time, stress, and surprise repairs later. Here are a few smart, handyman-approved ways to prepare your home for spring: 1. Check drainage around your home. After winter rains, make sure downspouts are clear and directing water away from your foundation. In older Piedmont homes, poor drainage is one of the most common – and preventable – causes of long-term damage. 2. Tune up doors and windows. If doors stick or windows feel drafty, it’s often a hinge or alignment issue – not a full replacement. A quick adjustment improves comfort and can lower energy bills as temperatures rise. 3. articles.text: Piedmont Community Church is committed to nurturing the next generation. The heart of NextGen is partnering with parents to help kids and teens develop a faith that truly sticks - one that shapes identity, builds resilience and guides everyday decisions as they grow up in a very challenging world. We want kids to know that they belong and are loved, supported and accepted for who they are. Adult leaders bring the stories of the Bible to life and connect scripture to kids’ lives. In small Life Groups, relationships grow, questions are welcomed and faith becomes personal. NextGen is lots of fun, with special holiday events for all ages as well as overnights, retreats and mission trips for older kids as part of our program. NOT JUST FOR KIDS It’s no secret that parenting today is more challenging than ever. Our NextGen Parent Life Group meets throughout the year to offer encouragement, connection and practical support. For more NextGen information, contact Kerry Perschitte at kerry@piedmontchurch.org Ultimately, we want all children and students to understand how God’s Word fits into their lives.
